title: American Wedding
full_review:
"American Wedding" (Universal) scrapes the bottom of the proverbial barrel for laughs, and what it comes up with is much of the same gunk found in the first two "American Pie" comedies.

Predictable and puerile, "American Wedding" is the third (and hopefully the last) installment of the comedy series which follows a group of young adults who spend most of their time talking about and obsessing over sex. In this film, college sweethearts Jim (Jason Biggs) and Michelle (Alyson Hannigan) decide to tie the knot, after Jim pops the question in a way most parents would find embarrassing to tell if their children ever asked. The whole gang, including Finch (Eddie Kaye Thomas), is therefore reunited for the upcoming nuptials -- even the obnoxious and foul-mouthed Stifler (Seann William Scott), one guest the happy couple would rather have forgotten.

The paper-thin plot revolves around the wedding preparations; however, the film's focus is not the betrothed pair, but Stifler. And so we have the tedious scenes of Stifler pretending to be a gentlemen -- attired in a preppy polo shirt and argyle vest -- as he tries to win over the bride's knock-out sister (January Jones); Stifler planning the depraved bachelor party; Stifler dancing at a gay bar; Stifler killing the elaborate flower arrangements; and finally, Stifler saving the day.

Apparently, the filmmakers must have thought that Scott's appeal was greater than the sum of the other characters to have placed him in the spotlight. But the problem with building the movie around the Stifler character is that Scott is neither believable nor appealing as he spews obscenities and makes gestures that would make even the most unflappable moviegoer blush.

The film is one long series of filler scenes. And most of the scenes include crude sex jokes or acts, telegraphed misunderstandings (usually sexual in nature) or lewd exchanges among the characters. The scenes, as well as being awful, lack originality and freshness. The jokes are lame. The actors seemingly are tired of playing the same daft characters. And the editing is choppy, as if director Jesse Dylan had no idea what to do with the mess by writer-producer Adam Herz.

The movie promos describe the characters as a "little more mature and ready to leap into their adult lives." But nothing could be further from the truth -- they each still have a childish view of sex and sexuality and deal with each other and situations in an immature manner. "American Wedding" is just a poor attempt at cashing in on the unfathomable appeal of the "American Pie" series. But this is one half-baked dessert no one is likely to want another piece of.

Because of several sexual encounters and countless crude sexual references, same-sex kissing, some nudity and repeated rough language with some profanity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
